clinicalPearls: The commonest congenital foot deformity of infancy, thought to reflect intrauterine moulding, giving a foot that curves inward at the forefoot while the hindfoot stays neutral
The forefoot is adducted and sometimes supinated, producing a C-shaped or bean-shaped lateral border with a prominent base of the fifth metatarsal
The heel bisector line normally passes through the second or third toe web; in metatarsus adductus it points more laterally toward the third to fifth toes, grading severity
Flexibility is the key clinical distinction: most feet can be passively abducted past the midline (mild) or to the midline (moderate), and only rigid feet resist correction
The vast majority resolve spontaneously without any intervention, so reassurance and observation are appropriate for flexible feet
There is a recognised association with developmental dysplasia of the hip, so the hips should always be examined and imaged if clinically indicated
Serial casting or reverse-last footwear is reserved for feet that remain rigid or fail to improve, and surgery is rarely needed
reference.pathophysiology: Metatarsus adductus is a transverse-plane deformity in which the metatarsals deviate medially at the tarsometatarsal joints while the hindfoot remains in normal alignment, distinguishing it from clubfoot which also involves hindfoot equinus and varus. It is generally regarded as a positional or packaging deformity resulting from crowding in utero, although imbalance of the medial soft tissues and abnormal insertion of the tibialis anterior or posterior have been implicated in more rigid forms. The medial soft tissues and the abductor hallucis may be tight, and in persistent cases bony adaptation of the medial cuneiform and metatarsal bases can develop, but the subtalar and ankle joints are typically unaffected.
additionalDifferentials: Clubfoot (congenital talipes equinovarus) with associated hindfoot equinus and varus
Skewfoot (serpentine foot) with forefoot adduction plus hindfoot valgus
Residual forefoot adduction following treated clubfoot
Metatarsus primus varus contributing to juvenile hallux valgus
Internal tibial torsion producing an in-toeing appearance without a true foot deformity
Neuromuscular forefoot deformity in conditions such as cerebral palsy
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment of forefoot flexibility and the heel bisector angle to grade severity
Examination of the hindfoot to exclude equinus and confirm a supple heel
Hip examination, with ultrasound or radiography where developmental dysplasia is suspected
Standing or simulated weight-bearing foot radiographs reserved for rigid or atypical deformity
Assessment of the contralateral foot and lower-limb rotational profile
Neurological examination to exclude an underlying neuromuscular cause in rigid or asymmetrical cases
redFlags: A rigid deformity that cannot be passively corrected, suggesting a structural rather than positional cause
Associated hindfoot equinus or varus indicating clubfoot rather than isolated forefoot adduction
Concurrent signs of hip dysplasia such as limited abduction or leg-length discrepancy
Progressive, painful, or markedly asymmetrical deformity, or features suggesting an underlying neuromuscular disorder
reference.prognosis: The outlook is excellent, as most flexible cases correct spontaneously within the first year or two of life; even moderate deformity usually responds well to serial casting, and long-term function and comfort are rarely impaired.
pitfalls: Mistaking metatarsus adductus for clubfoot by overlooking the normal, supple hindfoot
Failing to examine the hips and thereby missing coexisting developmental dysplasia
Overtreating flexible feet that would have resolved with simple observation
Delaying casting in the rare truly rigid foot, when earlier intervention is more effective
Confusing the condition with skewfoot, in which uncorrected hindfoot valgus needs recognition
management: Reassure and observe flexible feet, as the large majority correct spontaneously within the first years of life
Teach parents passive stretching exercises for mild to moderate flexible deformity
Apply serial casting for rigid or persistent deformity, with corrective footwear or orthoses following cast treatment
Reserve surgery for the rare severe rigid deformity persisting into later childhood
Examine the hips and image with ultrasound or radiography given the association with developmental dysplasia of the hip
Refer rigid, atypical, or asymmetrical cases to paediatric orthopaedics and exclude an underlying neuromuscular cause
Monitor foot alignment and growth over time
